lesson_title: The Ball That Bounced Off Tissue Paper
hook_text: In 1909 scientists fired particles at gold foil. Almost all went straight through. One in eight thousand came straight back. That discovery is why you have never touched anything.
clip_script: Manchester, 1909. Fire tiny, fast, positive particles at a sheet of gold foil just a few hundred atoms thick. If atoms are solid balls, the particles should struggle. Instead, almost every one sails straight through, as if the gold is not there. But about one in eight thousand comes flying back. Rutherford said it was like firing a shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back at you. The only explanation: the atom is almost entirely empty space, with a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus in the middle. Blow an atom up to the size of a stadium and the nucleus is a grain of sand on the centre spot, carrying nearly all the mass. Inside it, positive protons and neutral neutrons. Out in the emptiness, negative electrons, eighteen hundred times lighter. Equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the atom is neutral. And when you touch a table, your electrons are pushing on its electrons. You have never actually touched anything.
visual_style: A whiteboard sheet of gold foil with dotted particle paths streaming through and one arrow bouncing back; then a stadium outline with a single dot on the centre spot labelled nucleus.
pacing: Suspenseful setup, a sharp bounce-back moment, then a quick tour of the three particles and a punchy ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and count the particles in any atom.
